e.etymology: Popularized by the Mexican singer and telenovela actress known as Litzy, whose shows aired on US Spanish-language television in the early 2000s. It is generally taken as a pet form of Elizabeth, like Lizzy.
From Arabic khalid, 'eternal, everlasting', from khalada, 'to last forever'. Khalid ibn al-Walid was a famed general of early Islam. Khaled is the spelling common in Egypt and the Levant.
namesakes: Khaled Hosseini (author of The Kite Runner)

assoc.t: DJ Khaled, hip-hop producer and media personality

e.etymology: A respelling of Declan, the English form of Irish Deaglan, the name of a 5th-century saint who founded the monastery of Ardmore. Its meaning is uncertain; it is often read as 'full of goodness'.
Used in South Asian and Muslim families as a form of Rayyan, Arabic for 'lush, well-watered' and the name of a gate of Paradise in Islamic tradition. It also doubles as a spelling of Irish Ryan.
From the surname of actor Patrick Swayze, star of Dirty Dancing and Ghost. The surname is an English one of uncertain origin, also spelled Swasey.

assoc.t: Patrick Swayze, star of Dirty Dancing and Ghost

e.etymology: A respelling of Haisley, a modern American name that blends the sounds of Hailey, Hazel and Paisley. Haisley is also an uncommon surname.
A name with more than one source. In India it is Sanskrit laya, 'rhythm, musical tempo'. Elsewhere it is a spelling of Laia, the Catalan short form of Eulalia, or of Leia and Leya.
A respelling of Zayden, an American coinage of the 2000s that puts a Z on the sound of Aiden, Jayden and Kaden.
In Arabic haya means 'modesty, decency', a quality prized in Islam, and is a popular girls' name. In Hebrew, Haya, more often written Chaya, means 'living, alive'.
Latin caeli, 'of heaven', from caelum, 'sky, heaven', familiar to Catholics from the Marian hymn Regina Caeli, 'Queen of Heaven'. In everyday use it sounds like Kaylee.
The French word for love, from Latin amor. As a given name it is a recent American choice alongside Amor and Amora.
e.note: In English 'amour' can also mean a love affair, especially a secret one.

e.etymology: A modern American coinage in the Ky- family, close in sound to Zaire and Zyaire. Its parts have no set meaning.
A modern spelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Old French Cateline, itself a form of Catherine. In Irish it is said like Kathleen; English speakers read the spelling as KAYT-lin from the 1970s on.
namesakes: Caitlyn Jenner (Olympic decathlon champion and TV personality)

assoc.t: Caitlyn Jenner, Olympic champion and reality TV figure
Caitlyn, sharpshooter in League of Legends and Arcane

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Humbert, from Germanic hun, 'bear cub, young warrior', and berht, 'bright'. Its Italian form Umberto was borne by two kings of Italy.
The Ashkenazi and Yiddish pronunciation of Hebrew Avraham (Abraham), the first patriarch, whose name Genesis explains as 'father of a multitude'. It is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish communities.
From Hebrew Avi'el, joining avi, 'my father', and El, 'God'. English Bibles spell it Abiel, the name of King Saul's grandfather.
The English word artist, from French artiste and Latin ars, 'art, skill', taken up in the 2010s as a word name like Legend and Saint. Artis is an older name and surname with a similar sound.
From an English surname for someone from Leicester, the Midlands city whose Old English name ends in ceaster, 'Roman fort'. It became an American first name in the 1800s.
namesakes: Lester Flatt (bluegrass guitarist of Flatt and Scruggs)

e.etymology: From Latin Marcellinus, a pet form of Marcellus, itself a pet form of Marcus, a Roman name linked to the war god Mars. Several early saints bore it, including Pope Marcellinus.
A transliteration of Russian and Ukrainian Taya, the short form of Taisiya, a saint's name of Greek origin. In English it also fits the pattern of Maya and Kaya.
namesakes: Taya Kyle (author, widow of American Sniper Chris Kyle)

e.etymology: A spelling of Katya, the Russian pet form of Yekaterina (Catherine), from Greek Aikaterine. The -ia spelling is the usual one in Italian, French, Spanish and Portuguese.
A spelling of Josie, the pet form of Josephine, and occasionally of Joseph for boys. Joseph is Hebrew Yosef, 'he will add'.
namesakes: Josey Wales (Clint Eastwood's outlaw in The Outlaw Josey Wales)

assoc.t: Josey Wales, Clint Eastwood's outlaw gunfighter

e.etymology: The English word timber, from Old English timber, 'building, building material, wood'. It joined the outdoorsy word names of the 2010s.

assoc.t: 'Timber!', the logger's shout as a tree falls
Timber, 2013 hit song by Pitbull and Kesha

e.etymology: The English word soul, from Old English sawol, used as a given name since the 2010s. It sounds the same as Sol.

assoc.t: soul music, the genre of Aretha Franklin and Otis Redding

e.etymology: From an English surname meaning 'son of Ed', a short form of Edward or Edmund. It is common in Brazil, where it is linked to Thomas Edison; Pele was born Edson Arantes do Nascimento.
namesakes: Pele (soccer legend, born Edson Arantes do Nascimento)

e.etymology: A modern American blend of Kenzie, the short form of Mackenzie, with the -ley ending. It sits close to Kinsley and Kensley.
The Catalan short form of Eulalia, from Greek eu, 'well', and lalein, 'to speak'. Saint Eulalia is a patron saint of Barcelona, which keeps Laia among the favorite girls' names in Catalonia.
A Kikuyu name from Kenya meaning 'the happy one'. In the US it is also used as a spelling of McKenna, and Makena is the name of a beach on Maui.
In South Asian Muslim families, from Arabic sa'ira, 'traveler, wanderer'. In Hispanic families it is a variant of Zaira or Sara, also spelled Sayra.
The West African form of Fatima, the name of the Prophet Muhammad's daughter, by way of Fatimata. This French-style spelling is the usual one in Mali, Guinea and Senegal.
The Spanish and Italian form of Lysander, from Greek Lysandros, joining lysis, 'release', and aner, 'man'. Lysander was the Spartan admiral who won the Peloponnesian War.
A modern American name in the family of Aziah, Azariah and Aaliyah, with the popular -iyah ending. It has no established meaning of its own.
